name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTKINGDOM_MCQ_Q01 - Classification systems and taxonomic approaches

questiontext.text:
Match the classification systems or taxonomic approaches with their corresponding descriptions or proponents:

List IList II
(a) Artificial system(i) Given by Bentham and Hooker
(b) Natural system(ii) Uses chemical constituents of plants
(c) Numerical taxonomy(iii) Based mainly on vegetative characters or androecium structure
(d) Chemotaxonomy(iv) Uses computers to process all observable characters with equal importance

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle of Early Classification Systems
Artificial systems of classification used gross superficial morphological characters, such as habit, colour, number and shape of leaves, or the androecium structure (proposed by Linnaeus). Natural classification systems, such as the one given by George Bentham and Joseph Dalton Hooker for flowering plants, considered both external and internal affinities including ultrastructure, anatomy, embryology, and phytochemistry.

Step 2: Modern Taxonomic Tools
Numerical taxonomy is carried out using computers by assigning numbers and codes to all observable characters so that hundreds of characters can be processed with equal importance. Chemotaxonomy uses the chemical constituents of plants to resolve taxonomic confusions.

Step 3: Final Conceptual Matching
Artificial system pairs with based mainly on vegetative characters or androecium structure; Natural system pairs with given by Bentham and Hooker; Numerical taxonomy pairs with uses computers to process all observable characters with equal importance; and Chemotaxonomy pairs with uses chemical constituents of plants (a-iii, b-i, c-iv, d-ii).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTKINGDOM_MCQ_Q02 - Plant genera and their taxonomic groups

questiontext.text:
Match the following plant genera with their respective groups:

List IList II
(a) Chlamydomonas(i) Moss
(b) Cycas(ii) Pteridophyte
(c) Selaginella(iii) Algae
(d) Sphagnum(iv) Gymnosperm

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identification of Each Genus
Chlamydomonas is a unicellular green alga belonging to Chlorophyceae. Cycas is a gymnosperm characterised by unbranched stems, pinnate leaves, and naked seeds.

Step 2: Identification of Remaining Genera
Selaginella is a heterosporous pteridophyte bearing microphylls and strobili. Sphagnum is a bryophyte (specifically a moss) that provides peat.

Step 3: Final Conceptual Matching
Chlamydomonas pairs with Algae; Cycas pairs with Gymnosperm; Selaginella pairs with Pteridophyte; and Sphagnum pairs with Moss (a-iii, b-iv, c-ii, d-i).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTKINGDOM_MCQ_Q03 - Algal classes pigments and stored food

questiontext.text:
Match the algal classes or genera with their characteristic pigments, stored food, or commercial uses:

List IList II
(a) Chlorophyceae(i) Floridean starch and r-phycoerythrin
(b) Phaeophyceae(ii) Laminarin, mannitol, and algin
(c) Rhodophyceae(iii) Starch stored in pyrenoids
(d) Chlorella(iv) Protein-rich unicellular food supplement

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Characteristics of Algal Classes
Members of Chlorophyceae (green algae) possess chlorophyll a and b and store food primarily as starch in pyrenoids located within chloroplasts. Members of Phaeophyceae (brown algae) store complex carbohydrates as laminarin or mannitol and have a cellulosic wall covered by algin.

Step 2: Red Algae and Unicellular Supplements
Members of Rhodophyceae (red algae) have a predominance of the red pigment r-phycoerythrin and store food as floridean starch. Chlorella is a unicellular green alga rich in proteins and is used as a food supplement even by space travellers.

Step 3: Final Conceptual Matching
Chlorophyceae pairs with starch stored in pyrenoids; Phaeophyceae pairs with laminarin, mannitol, and algin; Rhodophyceae pairs with floridean starch and r-phycoerythrin; and Chlorella pairs with protein-rich unicellular food supplement (a-iii, b-ii, c-i, d-iv).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTKINGDOM_MCQ_Q04 - Algal reproduction modes and commercial products

questiontext.text:
Match the following algal genera with their characteristic mode of sexual reproduction or commercial product:

List IList II
(a) Ulothrix(i) Anisogamous sexual reproduction
(b) Eudorina(ii) Commercial source of agar
(c) Volvox(iii) Isogamous sexual reproduction with flagellated gametes
(d) Gelidium(iv) Oogamous sexual reproduction

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Modes of Sexual Reproduction in Algae
In Ulothrix, sexual reproduction is isogamous, involving the fusion of two flagellated gametes that are similar in size. In species of Eudorina, fusion occurs between two gametes dissimilar in size, which is termed anisogamous. In Volvox, fusion takes place between a large, non-motile female gamete and a smaller, motile male gamete, which is termed oogamous.

Step 2: Commercial Importance of Red Algae
Gelidium (along with Gracilaria) is a red alga from which agar is obtained commercially for growing microbes and preparing ice-creams and jellies.

Step 3: Final Conceptual Matching
Ulothrix pairs with isogamous sexual reproduction with flagellated gametes; Eudorina pairs with anisogamous sexual reproduction; Volvox pairs with oogamous sexual reproduction; and Gelidium pairs with commercial source of agar (a-iii, b-i, c-iv, d-ii).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTKINGDOM_MCQ_Q05 - Bryophyte structures and reproductive organs

questiontext.text:
Match the following bryophyte structures with their correct descriptions:

List IList II
(a) Gemmae(i) Flask-shaped female sex organ producing a single egg
(b) Protonema(ii) Creeping, green, branched, filamentous stage in mosses
(c) Antheridium(iii) Green, multicellular asexual buds in liverworts
(d) Archegonium(iv) Male sex organ producing biflagellate antherozoids

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Asexual and Vegetative Structures in Bryophytes
In liverworts such as Marchantia, asexual reproduction occurs via gemmae, which are green, multicellular asexual buds developing in gemma cups on the thalli. In mosses, the first stage of the gametophyte developing directly from a spore is the protonema, a creeping, green, branched, and frequently filamentous stage.

Step 2: Sex Organs in Bryophytes
Bryophytes have multicellular sex organs. The male sex organ is the antheridium, which produces biflagellate antherozoids. The female sex organ is the archegonium, which is flask-shaped and produces a single egg.

Step 3: Final Conceptual Matching
Gemmae pairs with green, multicellular asexual buds in liverworts; Protonema pairs with creeping, green, branched, filamentous stage in mosses; Antheridium pairs with male sex organ producing biflagellate antherozoids; and Archegonium pairs with flask-shaped female sex organ producing a single egg (a-iii, b-ii, c-iv, d-i).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTKINGDOM_MCQ_Q06 - Classes of pteridophytes and examples

questiontext.text:
Match the four classes of Pteridophyta with their representative genera:

List IList II
(a) Psilopsida(i) Equisetum
(b) Lycopsida(ii) Adiantum
(c) Sphenopsida(iii) Psilotum
(d) Pteropsida(iv) Selaginella

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Classification of Pteridophytes
Pteridophytes are classified into four distinct classes based on their morphological and anatomical features.

Step 2: Representative Genera of Each Class
Class Psilopsida is represented by Psilotum. Class Lycopsida includes Selaginella and Lycopodium. Class Sphenopsida is represented by Equisetum (horsetail). Class Pteropsida includes ferns such as Dryopteris, Pteris, and Adiantum.

Step 3: Final Conceptual Matching
Psilopsida pairs with Psilotum; Lycopsida pairs with Selaginella; Sphenopsida pairs with Equisetum; and Pteropsida pairs with Adiantum (a-iii, b-iv, c-i, d-ii).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTKINGDOM_MCQ_Q07 - Root associations and fertilisation events in seed plants

questiontext.text:
Match the following biological associations or fertilisation events in gymnosperms and angiosperms with their correct outcomes or partners:

List IList II
(a) Coralloid roots in Cycas(i) Triploid primary endosperm nucleus (PEN)
(b) Mycorrhiza in Pinus(ii) Fungal association with roots
(c) Triple fusion in angiosperms(iii) Diploid zygote formation
(d) Syngamy in angiosperms(iv) Association with N₂-fixing cyanobacteria

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Root Associations in Gymnosperms
In gymnosperms, roots are generally tap roots. In Pinus, the roots have a fungal association in the form of mycorrhiza. In Cycas, small specialised roots called coralloid roots are associated with nitrogen-fixing cyanobacteria.

Step 2: Double Fertilisation in Angiosperms
In angiosperms, two male gametes are discharged into the embryo sac. One male gamete fuses with the egg cell (syngamy) to form a diploid zygote. The other male gamete fuses with the diploid secondary nucleus (triple fusion) to produce the triploid primary endosperm nucleus (PEN), which develops into endosperm.

Step 3: Final Conceptual Matching
Coralloid roots in Cycas pairs with association with N₂-fixing cyanobacteria; Mycorrhiza in Pinus pairs with fungal association with roots; Triple fusion in angiosperms pairs with triploid primary endosperm nucleus (PEN); and Syngamy in angiosperms pairs with diploid zygote formation (a-iv, b-ii, c-i, d-iii).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTKINGDOM_MCQ_Q08 - Ploidy and nature of plant structures

questiontext.text:
Match the following plant cells or structures with their correct ploidy and biological nature:

List IList II
(a) Primary endosperm nucleus (dicot)(i) Diploid (2n), independent vascular plant body
(b) Leaf cell of a moss (Funaria)(ii) Triploid (3n), formed by triple fusion
(c) Sporophyte of a fern (Dryopteris)(iii) Haploid (n), part of the gametophyte
(d) Polar nuclei before fusion(iv) Two haploid (n) nuclei inside the embryo sac

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Analysis of Angiosperm Embryo Sac and Endosperm
In an angiosperm embryo sac, there are two haploid (n) polar nuclei that eventually fuse to form a diploid secondary nucleus. When a haploid male gamete fuses with this diploid secondary nucleus during triple fusion, it forms the triploid (3n) primary endosperm nucleus (PEN).

Step 2: Analysis of Moss and Fern Plant Bodies
In mosses such as Funaria, the dominant leafy plant body is the haploid (n) gametophyte, so its leaf cells are haploid (n). In contrast, in pteridophytes (ferns such as Dryopteris), the main plant body is a diploid (2n), independent vascular sporophyte.

Step 3: Final Conceptual Matching
Primary endosperm nucleus (dicot) pairs with triploid (3n), formed by triple fusion; Leaf cell of a moss pairs with haploid (n), part of the gametophyte; Sporophyte of a fern pairs with diploid (2n), independent vascular plant body; and Polar nuclei before fusion pairs with two haploid (n) nuclei inside the embryo sac (a-ii, b-iii, c-i, d-iv).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTKINGDOM_MCQ_Q09 - Plant life cycle patterns and exceptions

questiontext.text:
Match the following plant or algal genera with their corresponding life cycle patterns:

List IList II
(a) Spirogyra(i) Diplontic life cycle
(b) Fucus(ii) Haplontic life cycle
(c) Ectocarpus(iii) Haplo-diplontic life cycle (algal exception)
(d) Equisetum(iv) Haplo-diplontic with dominant vascular sporophyte

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Haplontic and Diplontic Algae
Most algae, including Volvox, Spirogyra, and some species of Chlamydomonas, exhibit a haplontic life cycle in which the free-living haploid gametophyte is dominant and the sporophyte is represented only by the one-celled zygote. However, the brown alga Fucus is an exception among algae and exhibits a diplontic life cycle.

Step 2: Haplo-diplontic Algae and Pteridophytes
While most algae are haplontic, genera such as Ectocarpus, Polysiphonia, and kelps exhibit a haplo-diplontic life cycle. All pteridophytes, such as Equisetum, exhibit a haplo-diplontic life cycle in which the diploid sporophyte is the dominant, independent, photosynthetic, vascular plant body.

Step 3: Final Conceptual Matching
Spirogyra pairs with haplontic life cycle; Fucus pairs with diplontic life cycle; Ectocarpus pairs with haplo-diplontic life cycle (algal exception); and Equisetum pairs with haplo-diplontic with dominant vascular sporophyte (a-ii, b-i, c-iii, d-iv).
